analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since February 2025 with no vote or hearing, and only three senators have signed on as cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to cap the interest rate on credit card borrowing at 10% a year, counting all finance charges. Card issuers that knowingly charge more would forfeit all interest on the debt, and cardholders could sue to recover interest and fees paid above the cap. Consumer regulators could also enforce the cap under existing law, and the cap would expire on January 1, 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry a credit card balance from month to month. Average card rates run well above 20%, so a 10% cap would roughly cut the interest cost of carrying a balance in half for tens of millions of people. The bill also lets borrowers who were overcharged sue to get all of the interest and fees back, and it preserves any stronger state-level caps.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit cards at 10%, inclusive of all finance charges.
Blocks issuers from evading the cap through fees: fees not counted as finance charges cannot be used to get around the 10% limit, and their total cannot exceed the finance charges assessed.
A creditor that knowingly charges above 10% forfeits the entire interest on the debt, and a cardholder can sue within two years to recover all interest, finance charges, or fees paid.
Violations are also subject to civil penalties under the Truth in Lending Act, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission.
States may keep or adopt stricter caps, since the bill does not override state laws that protect consumers more.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card companies, whose interest income from card balances would fall sharply. The honest cost on the other side is tighter credit: with a 10% ceiling, lenders would have less room to price for risk, so some borrowers — especially those with poor credit — could face lower limits, fewer offers, or a harder time getting a card at all. The cap is also temporary, so the relief ends in 2031.

drawbacks.text: The cap sunsets on January 1, 2031, so any relief is temporary and would need to be renewed by Congress.

A 10% ceiling sits well below the current average card rate, and lenders price cards for the risk that many borrowers will not repay. Capping the rate gives issuers less room to cover losses from borrowers who default, so lenders would likely respond by tightening credit — smaller limits and fewer approvals for the riskiest applicants. The bill tries to prevent issuers from recouping the difference through fees, and its fee limits are strict, which is exactly the pressure that would push lenders toward restricting access instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of cardholders who carry a balance, cutting rates from around 20% or more to 10% is a large, concrete saving, backed by real teeth — forfeiture of interest and a private right to sue. The main honest objection is access: the people most likely to lose something are risky borrowers, who could see credit dry up rather than get cheaper. The five-year sunset limits both the benefit and the disruption. On balance, the bill is a substantial transfer from card issuers to indebted households, with a real but narrower cost to marginal borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it, sent it to the Banking Committee, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 4, 2025, together with Sen. Josh Hawley.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history.
Three senators have cosponsored the bill: one Republican and two Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and banks, which keep charging prevailing rates of 20% or more because the bill never advanced. Cardholders carrying balances keep paying those rates.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted a 10% cap on credit card interest.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, has taken no recorded action on it — no hearing or markup appears in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by an independent with a Republican lead cosponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, so sponsorship is bipartisan, but the Republican-led Banking Committee has not acted and no vote has occurred to show where the parties stand.

industries.note: Card issuers earn the bulk of their profit from interest on revolving balances, much of it at rates above 20%. A 10% cap, with forfeiture of interest and a private right to sue for overcharges, would cut that revenue sharply; their interest in the bill runs against cardholders who carry debt.

analysis.trajectory: With four supporters out of 100 senators and no action in the Banking Committee more than a year into the Congress, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote. Rate-cap proposals have historically stalled at this stage, and the committee's agenda is controlled by the majority party.
